statement: In an unweighted graph, the depth at which depth-first search first discovers a vertex equals that vertex's shortest-path distance from the start vertex.
definitions: DFS = standard depth-first search from a start vertex s that recursively visits the first unvisited neighbour; a vertex's discovery depth is its depth in the resulting DFS tree (number of tree edges from s). Graph undirected, unweighted, connected. The counterexample may specify the order in which neighbours are examined; distance = length of a shortest path.
ground_truth_witness: Triangle on V = {s,a,b} with edges sa, ab, sb. DFS from s that visits neighbours in alphabetical order goes s (depth 0) -> a (depth 1) -> b (depth 2), so it records depth[b] = 2. The edge sb gives distance 1, which BFS reports. DFS commits to the first path it walks down, so its discovery depths can exceed the true distances.
reference_authority: online-cited counterexample (MO/MSE/CS.SE/Wikipedia) with verify script, verified per partB_feasibility records

skeptic.objection: False and the triangle witness is valid; verified that EVERY DFS neighbour order from s on the triangle discovers one of the other two vertices at depth 2 while its distance is 1, so the witness refutes the claim under both readings ('for every DFS execution' and 'for some execution'). The only ambiguity is what 'depth' means (DFS-tree depth) and whether the solver may fix the adjacency order; pin those. Elementary (difficulty 1) but a real trace, and the roster has only one traversal item (BFS bipartiteness).
